notes: Ruling slot 22 holds UPRONA (MD places it in 20, but it is the governing single party of Micombero's military republic). Coalition slot 13 holds the army. Slot 20 becomes the Tutsi-Hima Bururi clique. MD's FRODEBU, UPD and CNDD (1990s) are anachronistic and replaced; slot 23 keeps the House of Ntwero with Ntare V.

0.name: Abaganwa
0.text:
The Abaganwa are the princely caste of Burundi, descendants of former kings divided into the rival Bezi and Batare lineages. Under Belgian rule they supplied most of the chiefs, and they remain wealthy in land and cattle, though the 1966 republic stripped them of their political role.

They favour an ordered, hierarchical society, close ties with Belgium and the Catholic missions, and firm anti-communism. Many accept the republic only as a lesser evil to Hutu power. Their base lies in the old chieftaincies and among educated princely families, and their leverage rests on land, prestige in the hills and family ties to officials and officers.

1.name: Parti Démocrate Chrétien
1.text:
The Christian Democratic Party was founded in 1959 by Batare princes, the sons of Chief Pierre Baranyanka, and favoured by the Belgian administration as a rival to UPRONA. Its leaders Joseph Biroli and Jean-Baptiste Ntidendereza were executed in 1963 for the assassination of Prince Louis Rwagasore, and the party has been banned since 1966.

The PDC tradition stands for Christian social teaching, private property, gradual development and close friendship with Belgium and the West. Its remaining sympathisers are Batare loyalists, Catholic notables and conservative officials. Its leverage lies in princely landholdings in the north and in the Belgian connections that still matter in Bujumbura.

2.name: Groupe de Monrovia
2.text:
The Monrovia Group is the moderate wing of UPRONA, named after the moderate African bloc of 1961, which united Hutu politicians and liberal Tutsi in the early years of independence. Its leaders were struck down one after another: Prime Minister Pierre Ngendandumwe was assassinated in 1965 and Paul Mirerekano executed after the failed coup of that year.

Its survivors call for parliamentary government, fair representation of Hutu in the state, an end to ethnic purges and friendship with the West. After the alleged Hutu plot of 1969 and the executions that followed, they live in silence. Their leverage lies in the support of a Hutu majority excluded from power.

3.name: Parti du Peuple
3.text:
The People's Party was founded in 1959 as the first party speaking explicitly for Burundi's Hutu majority, inspired by the social revolution next door in Rwanda. Weak in elections against UPRONA, it was dissolved with all other parties after the 1966 coup, and many of its cadres have since been imprisoned or killed.

Its tradition calls for social justice, land reform, schooling and jobs for the Hutu, and a democratic government based on the majority. It looks to Western social democracy and Catholic social teaching rather than to Moscow. Its base lies among Hutu teachers, clerks and catechists, and its leverage rests on their bitterness and their contacts among the Hutu peasantry.

4.name: Cercle Marxiste
4.text:
The Marxist Circle is a small group of students and young teachers at the Official University of Bujumbura, founded in 1964, and of Burundians returned from scholarships in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. They read Lenin and the Soviet press in private homes in Bujumbura.

They argue that ethnic politics hide a class struggle and call for a planned economy, nationalised trade, collective farming and an alliance with the socialist camp. They reject both the Tutsi military clique and Hutu sectarianism. Their influence is small, but their leverage lies in student circles and in contacts with the Soviet embassy and East European trade missions.

5.name: Les Mulelistes
5.text:
The Mulelists are Hutu radicals and young exiles inspired by Pierre Mulele's peasant rebellion in the Congo, many of whom fled after the purges of 1965 and 1969 to Tanzania, Rwanda and the Congo. Some have mixed with Congolese rebels still active across Lake Tanganyika.

They preach armed insurrection against the Tutsi-led military regime, the arming of peasants and the overthrow of the Bururi clique, mixing revolutionary slogans with ethnic grievance. They have no single leader or open organisation. Their leverage lies in exile networks along the lake shore and the south, and in the anger of Hutu families who lost relatives in the executions.

6.name: Groupe de Casablanca
6.text:
The Casablanca Group is the radical Tutsi wing of UPRONA, named after the revolutionary African bloc of Nkrumah and Nasser, which fought the moderates in the early 1960s. Its leaders, such as André Muhirwa, admired Lumumba and welcomed ties with China before Beijing's embassy was expelled in 1965.

The group stands for an uncompromising nationalism, hostility to Belgian and American influence, a strong single party and close ties with the radical and socialist states. It defends Tutsi dominance in the name of anti-colonial unity. Its base lies among Tutsi intellectuals and party veterans in Bujumbura, and its leverage rests on their place in the party and ministries.

7.name: Jeunesse Révolutionnaire Rwagasore
7.text:
The Rwagasore Revolutionary Youth is the youth movement of UPRONA, named after the assassinated founder Prince Louis Rwagasore and turned into a mass organisation after the 1966 revolution. Its brigades patrol Bujumbura and the provinces, watch schools and denounce suspected enemies of the republic.

The JRR uses anti-imperialist and revolutionary rhetoric, praising the abolition of the monarchy and calling for a disciplined nation under the party and President Micombero. Its activists are mostly young Tutsi from the schools and towns. Its leverage lies in its role as the regime's street force and informant network, which makes it feared by Hutu pupils, teachers and civil servants.

8.name: Ismaili Jamat of Bujumbura
8.text:
The Ismaili Jamat of Bujumbura is the small community of Shia Ismaili traders of Indian origin settled in Burundi's capital, followers of the Aga Khan. Its families run import firms, shops and transport businesses along the lake trade route to Kigoma and Dar es Salaam.

The community promotes modern education, health care and economic self-help under the Aga Khan's progressive guidance, while staying loyal to whoever governs. It avoids political involvement entirely. Its leverage lies in its capital and commercial networks, its links to the wealthier Ismaili communities of Tanzania, Uganda and Kenya, and its importance to the supply of goods in a landlocked country.

9.name: Wapenzi wa Ahl al-Bayt
9.text:
The Devotees of the Prophet's House are a small circle of Twelver Shia traders and their sons in Bujumbura, linked to the Khoja communities of Dar es Salaam and Zanzibar and to clerics in Najaf. They follow Grand Ayatollah Muhsin al-Hakim and import religious books from Iraq and India.

They call for strict religious observance, the authority of the learned clergy and the defence of Islam against secular and Western ways. Their weight in Burundian politics is negligible, but their leverage lies in their commercial wealth and in ties to East African Shia networks that are beginning to send preachers and money into the interior.

10.name: Waislamu wa Buyenzi
10.text:
The Muslims of Buyenzi are the Swahili-speaking community of Bujumbura's Muslim quarter and of the lake towns of Rumonge and Nyanza-Lac, descended from coastal traders, Congolese migrants and Burundian converts. They gather around their imams, mosques and Quranic schools.

Their elders practise a quiet, conservative Sunni Islam loyal to the authorities, seeking recognition alongside the churches, access to schools and support for pilgrimage. They keep clear of the ethnic conflict that divides the country. Their leverage lies in their role in Bujumbura's commerce, transport and crafts and in good relations with Muslim states such as Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

11.name: Wito wa Khalifa
11.text:
The Call of the Caliphate is a tiny circle of young Muslims in Buyenzi who returned from studies in Cairo, Khartoum and Mecca with pan-Islamic tracts and radical sermons. They meet in private, wary of both their own elders and the JRR's informers.

They reject ethnic politics, nationalism and both the Western and Soviet camps as false idols, and dream of a worldwide Muslim community governed by Islamic law under a restored caliphate. They have no recognised leader and little following. Their leverage lies in the frustration of young Muslims excluded from Catholic schools and state jobs, and in literature and money arriving from abroad.

12.name: Umoja wa Vijana wa Kiislamu
12.text:
The Muslim Youth Union is a reformist association of young Muslim teachers, clerks and traders in Bujumbura who want to modernise their community. They draw on Egyptian reformist writings and the example of Muslim associations in Tanzania and Kenya.

They call for Muslim schools combining religion and modern subjects, scholarships, charity for the poor and recognition of Islam in public life, and criticise corruption and the moral decline of the towns. They avoid confrontation with the regime. Their leverage lies in their education, their growing role as spokesmen for Burundian Muslims and their links to Arab embassies and donors.

13.name: Armée Burundaise
13.text:
The Burundian Army grew from the colonial Force Publique units and was trained by Belgian officers. Captain Michel Micombero used it to abolish the monarchy in November 1966, and since the purges of 1965 and 1969, when Hutu officers were executed for alleged plots, its officer corps is almost entirely Tutsi.

The officers stand for order, discipline and the defence of the republic against both monarchists and Hutu rebellion, and rely on Belgian training and equipment. Southern Tutsi-Hima from Bururi dominate the command. Their leverage lies in their monopoly of arms and in the fact that the regime is, at its core, a government of the army.

14.name: Église catholique au Burundi
14.text:
The Catholic Church in Burundi is the country's largest institution after the state, with most of the population baptised and most schools, hospitals and missions in its hands. It is led by André Makarakiza, Archbishop of Gitega, alongside European missionaries of the White Fathers.

The Church stands for Christian morality, Catholic education and social peace between Hutu and Tutsi, and avoids open conflict with the military regime. It remains outside the Cold War blocs while looking to Rome and Belgium. Its base lies in parishes and seminaries, and its leverage rests on schools that train the elite and on missionaries who see more of the hills than the government does.

15.name: Les Barons du Café
15.text:
The Coffee Barons are the exporters, merchants and officials who control the trade in coffee, the source of most of Burundi's export earnings. Belgian, Greek and Asian trading houses work with well-placed Tutsi officials and officers in Bujumbura to buy from millions of peasant growers.

They want stable coffee prices, export licences, cheap credit and a government that keeps the hills quiet and the growers producing. They are pragmatic about politics and close to the ruling clique. Their leverage lies in their hold over the country's foreign exchange and the commissions that finance officials, the party and many careers in the army.

16.name: Chambre de Commerce de Bujumbura
16.text:
The Bujumbura Chamber of Commerce gathers the merchants, importers and small industrialists of the capital, Burundi's only real town and port on Lake Tanganyika. Belgian, Greek, Asian and Arab traders sit beside the first Burundian businessmen.

They call for free trade, low duties, secure property and an end to arbitrary levies and favouritism toward the regime's friends. They fear state monopolies and ethnic purges that disrupt business. Their leverage lies in their role in supplying the country through the lake and the roads to Tanzania, Rwanda and the Congo, and in the customs revenues the treasury depends on.

17.name: Gardiens de la Kibira
17.text:
The Guardians of the Kibira are foresters, agronomists and missionary naturalists who defend the Kibira mountain forest along the Congo-Nile ridge, the last great forest of an overcrowded country, and the shores of Lake Tanganyika. Many trained under Belgian forestry and agricultural research services.

They warn that land clearing, erosion and overpopulation are destroying Burundi's soils and water, and call for forest reserves, reforestation and protection of chimpanzees and lake fish. They have no political organisation. Their leverage lies in their technical expertise, the support of Belgian and international aid agencies and the evident danger of erosion on the hills.

18.name: Union des Travailleurs du Burundi
18.text:
The Union of Burundian Workers is the single trade union federation created in 1967 to replace the independent unions dissolved after the 1966 revolution, and it is tied to UPRONA. It organises dock workers, transport workers, civil servants and employees of Bujumbura's few factories.

The UTB speaks for African socialism, wage protection, workers' housing and national control of the economy, within the limits set by the party. Its rank and file include many Hutu workers who remember the independent unions crushed in the 1960s. Its leverage lies in the capacity of the Bujumbura port and civil service to stop work, a pressure the regime cannot ignore.

19.name: Les Pékinois
19.text:
The Pekingese are the pro-Chinese militants of Bujumbura who flourished in 1963–64, when Beijing's embassy used Burundi as a base for supporting rebels in the Congo and Rwanda. After the embassy was expelled in 1965, its friends among radical politicians, teachers and students went quiet but did not disappear.

They admire Mao's peasant revolution and call for people's war, self-reliance and the overthrow of feudal and imperialist structures, rejecting Soviet revisionism. Their leverage lies in contacts with Chinese diplomats in Dar es Salaam, with Congolese rebels across the lake and with young radicals who see Burundi's crisis as a class struggle.

20.name: Groupe de Bururi
20.text:
The Bururi Group is the clique of Tutsi-Hima officers and officials from the southern province of Bururi, Micombero's home region, who have taken control of the army, the party and key ministries. Its hardliners include Arthémon Simbananiye and Albert Shibura, architects of the purges against Hutu officers and politicians.

The group preaches national unity in words while defending Tutsi-Hima dominance, treating any Hutu political demand as a plot and distrusting the old Ganwa aristocracy. Its base lies in the southern officer corps and the JRR, and its leverage rests on its grip on the security services and its willingness to use extreme force to keep power.

21.name: Jeunesse Nationaliste Rwagasore
21.text:
The Rwagasore Nationalist Youth was the militant Tutsi youth group of the early 1960s that attacked Hutu trade unionists and politicians in Bujumbura's Kamenge district in January 1962. Officially succeeded by the party's youth movement, its veterans form a hard core of ultras within the JRR and the security services.

They preach the defence of the nation and the revolution by force, total loyalty to the leader and the elimination of Hutu leadership as a threat to the state, scorning parliamentary politics and foreign advice. Their base lies among urban Tutsi youth and former activists, and their leverage rests on their readiness to carry out violence for the regime.

22.name: Union pour le Progrès National
22.text:
The Union for National Progress was founded in 1958 by Prince Louis Rwagasore and led Burundi to independence before his assassination in 1961. Since the coup of November 1966 it has been the single party of the military republic headed by President Michel Micombero, who rules through the party, the army and the National Revolutionary Council.

UPRONA invokes Rwagasore's legacy of national unity, anti-colonialism and progress, while serving as the instrument of a Tutsi-dominated military regime that crushed alleged Hutu plots in 1969. It cooperates with Belgium and France while courting radical African states. Its leverage rests on its monopoly of politics, its youth wing and the army behind it.

23.name: House of Ntwero
23.text:
The House of Ntwero is the royal dynasty that ruled the Kingdom of Burundi for centuries until the monarchy was abolished by Micombero's coup of 28 November 1966. Its head, Mwami Ntare V, who had deposed his father Mwambutsa IV only months earlier, now lives in exile in West Germany.

The royalists call for the restoration of the crown as a symbol above ethnic division, a constitutional monarchy and reconciliation between Hutu and Tutsi under the mwami. Their base lies among Ganwa families, rural elders and Hutu who remember the crown as a protector. Their leverage rests on the residual sacred prestige of the mwami in the hills.
